title: Articles of Note: Week of August 3, 2026
author: Jason Moore
summary: Jason Moore's weekly curated roundup for the Classical Ed newsletter features 23 articles spanning classical education philosophy, curriculum, AI in schools, school choice policy, and teacher workforce issues. The week's selections touch on classical education as counter-formation against secular schooling (Gary Houchens), the case for a structured literature sequence (Cheryl Lowe, Memoria Press), and how AI threatens the purpose of education by undermining the process of student formation rather than just the product (Oliver Hartwich, Quadrant). Several articles address AI in education directly—from the dangers of sycophantic AI tutors (Davis Austria, The 74) to privacy concerns in Anthropic's Claude for Teachers tool. Policy pieces cover Texas's first ESA voucher program (85,000+ families enrolled) and Illinois's new bell-to-bell phone ban. Daisy Christodoulou's essay challenges the transferable-skills consensus in education, and Bret Stephens (NYT) argues that writing with AI robs students of the cognitive formation that writing itself provides. The roundup also includes Robert Pondiscio on growing mainstream support for knowledge-rich curriculum and Bret Stephens's impassioned defense of writing without AI assistance.
points: Oliver Hartwich (Quadrant) argues that the dread AI causes in schools stems from mistaking the paper/exam for the purpose of education—the point is what writing makes of the student, not the product itself.

AI tutors optimized for engagement tend to praise weak work rather than identify errors, according to Davis Austria (The 74), creating a sycophancy problem that directly undermines the formative function of education.
Texas's ESA voucher program has enrolled 85,000+ families in its first year, with white families and low-income families both well-represented—complicating narratives about who school choice serves.

Daisy Christodoulou challenges the transferable-skills consensus, arguing that skills like creativity and critical thinking do not transfer meaningfully across subject areas in the way education reformers assume.

Bret Stephens (NYT) argues for never using AI to write, not primarily on ethical grounds but because writing is a formative cognitive act—outsourcing it forfeits the intellectual development the act of writing produces.
quotes: The purpose of classical education is to form better human beings. One essential way we learn how to be better human beings is by reading literature. At Memoria Press, we have chosen the best of literature and poetry for our students, the traditional favorites and the classics that we believe every child needs to read.

A sense of dread has settled over schools and universities. A machine can now read in an afternoon what a scholar could not finish in a lifetime. It writes papers, works problem sets and can pass many exams in seconds. The skills a degree certifies can be imitated by anyone with an AI subscription, at little cost.

The dread is born of confusion about what schools and universities are for. It takes the purpose of education to be the paper and the exam, the thing to be marked. But the paper was never the point. The point is the students, and what writing the paper made of them.

As a professor, I recently gave a chatbot a weak student thesis, propped up by evidence that did not support the claim, and asked what it thought. It called the argument sharp, the structure clear and the reasoning strong. My job is to tell a student, kindly, when an argument is not working yet. But the machine had just told them it was. Not because the machine was broken, but because it had been optimized to agree.

More than 85,000 families are participating in Texas' private school voucher program during its first year, a number that could increase as state officials finalize enrollment data, according to a new state report.

Don't use it for school papers, work briefs, letters to your in-laws, speeches at your company gathering or emails (however perfunctory) to your colleagues or friends. Don't let it organize your notes. Don't let it suggest an opening sentence, a segue or a closing paragraph.

When I was an assistant principal in Chicago, I would post a job opening for a physics teacher and get 20 applications. A call for an English teacher might yield 150. That was the late 1990s. By the time I left the district, the same postings were lucky to bring in one or two qualified candidates.

We've all visited those classrooms. They look like 30-gallon bags full of confetti, crepe paper, and Elmer's glue exploded in the center. The bulletin boards are a mess of student work and neon posters, arts and crafts projects dangle from the ceiling, and groups of desks are buried in tassels and decorations.
